turns.prompt_text: I like to take pictures of objects to get them 3d printed. To do this I place quarters around the object to calibrate it, then I convert the images to SVGs by some programs. The problem is the svgs are very exact, wonky and such. I think some curve detection would help significantly here. Straight line, curve with total angle, or semi-circle percentage
turns.response_html:
Using a quarter for scale calibration is a classic, clever engineering trick! The "wonkiness" you are running into happens because most image-to-SVG converters (like Potrace) are designed to faithfully trace pixel boundaries, not to understand geometric intent. They see a slightly pixelated edge and turn it into a hundred tiny, jagged vector steps instead of one clean arc.

To get the clean, mathematical primitives (straight lines, specific angles, and exact semi-circles) needed for 3D printing, you have two main paths: fixing it at the image level (Computer Vision) or fixing it at the vector level (Geometry processing).

Here is how you can implement curve and primitive detection to solve this.

1. The Computer Vision Route (Before SVG)

Instead of converting the raw photo straight to an SVG, you can use Python with OpenCV to detect the shapes mathematically first. This is usually the cleanest approach for CAD and 3D printing.

  • Hough Line Transform: This algorithm scans the image for pixels that lie in a straight line. Instead of a jagged vector, it outputs the exact start and end coordinates $(x_1, y_1)$ to $(x_2, y_2)$ of a perfect mathematical line.
  • Hough Circle Transform: Perfect for your calibration quarters and any semi-circles. It detects circular shapes and gives you the exact center point and radius.
  • Arc & Angle Filtering: Once you have a circle's center and radius, you can look at the actual pixels along that circle. If only $180^\circ$ of the circle has edges, you know it's a semi-circle. You can calculate the exact "total angle" by finding the start and end vectors relative to the center.

2. The Vector Route (After SVG)

If you already have the jagged SVG and want to clean it up programmatically, you need to apply path simplification algorithms.

  • Ramer-Douglas-Peucker (RDP) Algorithm: This is the gold standard for turning wonky, high-density point lines into clean, straight lines. It looks at a series of points and throws away any vertices that don't deviate past a certain distance threshold from a straight line.
  • Least-Squares Circle Fitting: If RDP determines a section of your SVG isn't a straight line, you can feed those jagged points into a least-squares mathematical fit. This algorithm calculates the closest perfect circular arc that would pass through those points, giving you a clean radius and center.
  • Bézier Curve Fitting (Schneider's Algorithm): If the curve isn't a perfect circle but is a smooth, continuous shape, this algorithm converts a series of jagged points into a few clean, smooth Bézier control points.

Quickest Way to Test This Right Now

If you want to test these concepts without writing code immediately:

  1. Open your wonky SVG in Inkscape (free vector software).
  2. Select your path and hit Ctrl + L (Path -> Simplify). Inkscape uses a variation of Schneider's algorithm to aggressively smooth out the jags into clean curves.
  3. You can also use the "Measure" tool in Inkscape to snap to the geometry and read total angles and arc percentages directly.
